Remember, all of the components on these cards are representations of aircraft relays and breakers which would be controlled in flight by a flight computer.
Also seen on the card are representations of DC to AC static inverters. Some loads on aircraft require AC power and these devices convert the DC to AC from the generator bus.

The emergency bus connects directly to the essential busses. This bus can be powered by the generator bus or directly from the battery through S3. If a generator bus becomes damaged, this is an alternate route for power.

The second bus connects to the essential and emergency busses. This is the most important bus of the Split-Bus Distribution system. The battery switch connects or disconnects battery power to this bus.

Switch S1 is a non-essential disconnect switch. This removes all power from the non-essential loads. This is important when power is limited. Remember, the non-essential bus applies power to loads that are not necessary for safe flight.
The only time the busses would need to be connected is if one of the generators became faulty and were disconnected from the system.
In normal operation this switch should be in the NC (not connected) position. This in effect separates the two busses from each other.
The next two busses, bus 1 and bus 2, are the generator busses. The input to these busses is the output from the generators. Notice that there is a switch between the two busses.
S2 and S3 are the switches used to distribute the power from the battery. Remember, the battery should only be used to start the aircraft or when the aircraft generators fail.
There are seven different busses represented on this card. The bus to the far left is the battery bus. This bus connects the battery output to the generator 2 and emergency busses.
The PC130-736 card is the Split-Bus Distribution system. Pick it up and examine it.
Switches S1 and S2 are used to turn on and off the output of the generators. The output we will be using is two 12 volt DC sources.
Pick up and examine the PC130-735 card. This card is the AC to DC generator system which provides two balanced DC voltages. We will be using both voltage sources for this experiment...
The circuits are mounted on two circuit cards. The controls, components and indicators represent different sections of an aircraft Split-Bus system.
In this experiment, you will look at the basic operation of a Split- Bus Distribution system. By understanding this operation, troubleshooting of a faulty system can be quick and effective.

As you can see there are many advantages to using the Split-Bus Power Distribution system. The diagrams below illustrate some other common power distribution configurations.

Most aircraft have special socketed plugs that prevent power from being connected to the aircraft incorrectly. The external power switching unit provides extra protection against incorrect power connection.

Both bus tie switching units are connected so power flows from the external power source to all loads on the system. If external power is connected incorrectly, a relay unit prevents it from being connected to the buses.

When an aircraft is on the ground and engines are off, external power is required. External power is applied to the same line as the auxiliary generator. The generator switching units are not connected so power doesn't flow to the generator.

Changing the position of the switching system applies the power from the auxiliary generator to the second transfer bus. Now each bus is again independent. On certain systems non-essential loads can be reattached to the system.

By connecting the 2nd bus tie switching unit, power is supplied to the bus of generator two. Since the switching system is still connected to the 1st generator's bus, power from the auxiliary generator is not connected to the 2nd transfer bus yet.

The auxiliary generator will be started. The auxiliary power switching unit is now connected, but power is still not applied to the bus. We need to apply power from the auxiliary generator to the 2nd generator's bus.

It is important to know that in most Split-Bus systems when a generator fails, all non-essential loads are automatically disconnected from the system. This prevents overloading the remaining generator.

To get power from generator 1 to the loads that generator 2 supplies power to; the Bus Switching System of generator 2 is used. The switching unit of generator 2 (G2) is disconnected and the Bus Switching System is changed connecting
generator 2's loads to generator 1's output.
Now let's say that generator 2 becomes faulty and we haven't started the auxiliary generator. We need to disconnect
generator 2 from the bus and some how connect power to the loads of generator 2.

Generalized Split-BUS Power Distribution
TRY AGAIN!
All generators in the Split-Bus Distribution system are all connected to the same bus.

The operation of Generator 2 is identical to Generator 1. The Bus tie switching units are used when auxiliary power is needed. The Auxiliary generator switching unit is not connected, which means the Auxiliary generator is not connected to the bus.

Power then flows from the generator bus, through another switching system, to the load attached to the transfer bus. The Bus Switching system is used to transfer power between generators in case one generator fails.

Let's analyze the operation of our generalized Split-Bus system. Both main generators are supplying power and their associated switching unit is connected. From generator one, power is applied to the generator bus, but not through the bus tie switching unit.

These different switching units include bus tie breakers, generator breakers, and bus switching systems. In this lesson they will be referred to as switching units to simplify the operation of the Split-Bus system.

The picture below illustrates a generalized Split-Bus Power Distribution system. As you can see there are two main generators, and an auxiliary generator. There are also many switching units that connect and disconnect different sections of the bus.
Most Split-Bus Power Distribution systems contain an auxiliary generator for emergency situations. This generator does not generate power until it has been started either automatically or manually.
The Split-Bus Power Distribution system differs from other systems, in that it is two or more independent systems. Each generator powers its own bus, meaning the various loads are "Split" up.
